title: One Hyperplane to Rule the Brain?: Rosenblatt's Single-Layer Perceptron, the Minsky–Papert XOR Reckoning, and the Deep Feature-Learning Revolution — Why Frank Rosenblatt's 1958 Mark I Perceptron and finite-mistake convergence theorem sparked AI's first connectionist euphoria; Marvin Minsky & Seymour Papert's 1969 convexity & group-invariance proof against single-layer XOR and topological connectedness plus Mikel Olazaran's sociological audit of how credit-assignment pessimism froze neural funding; Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams's 1986 Nature backpropagation breakthrough, George Cybenko's 1989 Universal Approximation Theorem & Cortes & Vapnik's 1995 Support-Vector kernel lifting; plus Ghorbani, Mei, Misiakiewicz & Montanari's 2021 proof that frozen 'lazy' NTK/random-feature perceptrons still fail without active multi-layer feature learning

teenKit.tldr: In 1958, a massive mechanical machine called the Perceptron made people think artificial intelligence was instantly ready to conquer the human mind, only for a brutal mathematical reality check to freeze neural network research for fifteen years.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Understanding how a single math limitation can completely kill a technology helps us separate real breakthroughs from modern tech hype when looking at today's AI tools.
keyTakeaways: Frank Rosenblatt's 1958 Mark I Perceptron used physical motors and wires to learn visual patterns, proving simple neural models could learn from mistakes on basic categories.
Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert proved in 1969 that single-layer networks mathematically failed at basic logic problems like XOR, unfairly causing a 15-year funding freeze for the whole field.

Modern AI only recovered when scientists figured out how to train multi-layer networks using backpropagation, allowing computers to finally learn complex features instead of just memorizing surface data.

vocab.meaning: The simplest possible artificial neural network designed to sort data into two distinct categories using a single line or plane.
A basic logic puzzle where an output is only true if inputs are different, which completely stumped early single-layer AI models.
An algorithm that feeds prediction errors backward through a network to adjust hidden weights and make the system smarter over time.
A mathematical framework showing that frozen or lazy random networks struggle with high-dimensional data unless they actively learn features across multiple layers.

quiz.question: What physical hardware did Frank Rosenblatt's 1958 Mark I Perceptron rely on to adjust its learned weights?
options: Fiber optic cables and quantum processors
Magnetic hard drives and vacuum tubes only
quiz.explanation: The 1958 machine was a noisy mechanical beast that literally used motorized parts to physically grind gears and adjust potentiometers when making mistakes.

quiz.question: Why did the 1969 book by Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert cause an 'AI winter'?
options: They proved mathematically that single-layer perceptrons could not solve basic logical tasks like XOR parity.
They stole all the research funding to build competing supercomputers.
They convinced the US government that computers were physically incapable of running code.
They proved that multi-layer networks were permanently impossible to build.
quiz.explanation: Their mathematical proof showed the hard limits of single-layer networks on XOR and connectedness, leading to widespread pessimism and a 15-year funding drought.

quiz.question: According to modern 2021 research by Ghorbani, Mei, Misiakiewicz, and Montanari, what is required to defeat the curse of dimensionality in deep learning?
options: Larger datasets with zero human curation
Active multi-layer feature learning instead of frozen or lazy random features
Reverting back to the original 1958 Mark I analog design
quiz.explanation: Their work proved that frozen or 'lazy' models still fail without active multi-layer feature learning to dynamically transform complex data.
